knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scheduler metadata jointly determines eligibility from timing, frequency, depth, and delay settings, then orders eligible separators by priority subject to ties and early termination.
assumptions_latex: The solver defines the frequency predicate and delayed-execution policy.
Metadata are read consistently throughout one scheduling decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The eligible set is determined by the nonpriority fields of \(M_s\), while \(p_s\) orders its members.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected condition kind fits a scheduler metadata contract, but the metadata tuple, eligibility conjunction, priority direction, and permitted early termination are implementation-specific claims without cited evidence.

children.title: User-Cut Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces for optional relaxation strengthening without changing the intended feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Node User Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of globally valid inequalities at a fractional node relaxation solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a node relaxation \(R_N\), its optimal fractional solution \(\bar x\), and a separation oracle for inequalities valid for every integer-feasible solution in the cut's declared scope. Query the oracle at \(\bar x\). For each returned inequality \(a^\top x\le b\), verify validity for that scope and violation \(a^\top\bar x>b+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\ge0\) is the numerical tolerance; submit each admissible inequality through the user-cut interface. If cuts are accepted, reoptimize the relaxation and repeat according to the solver's round limit; otherwise stop and return the current relaxation state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fractional node solution, separate valid violated inequalities, submit admissible ones as user cuts, and reoptimize until no cut is accepted or a round limit applies.
assumptions_latex: The node relaxation has an available solution \(\bar x\).
The oracle returns inequalities valid for the declared cut scope.
The solver supplies a violation tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every submitted cut excludes \(\bar x\) beyond tolerance without excluding any integer-feasible point in its declared scope.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the fractional-node separation container, and the validity and violation tests are standard. The cited valid-cuts section does not establish the claimed user-cut callback submission, acceptance, reoptimization, or round-limit behavior, so an authoritative callback or solver-interface source is required.

children.title: Global User Cuts
children.top_down_role: User-cut submission for cuts valid throughout the search tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Global User Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: User cuts valid throughout the complete branch-and-bound tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of the original mixed-integer model. A submitted inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) is a global user cut if \(a^\top x\le b\) holds for every \(x\in F\), independently of the current node's local bounds or branching decisions. Once admitted, the inequality may therefore be enforced at the current node, inherited by descendants, and reused at any other node without a validity check tied to local ancestry. Global validity does not imply that the cut is violated, numerically stable, or beneficial enough for admission.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global user cut is valid for every feasible solution of the original model, so it may be used anywhere in the search tree.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) denotes the original model's feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut is global exactly when \(F\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^\top x\le b\}\).

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Local User Cuts
children.top_down_role: User-cut submission for cuts restricted to a node or subtree.

knowledge_statements.title: Local User Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: User cuts whose validity depends on the current node's local domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the original feasible set and let \(D_N\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) encode the local bounds and branching decisions at node \(N\). An inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) is a local user cut at \(N\) if it is valid on \(F\cap D_N\), but global validity on \(F\) is not asserted. The cut may be enforced at \(N\) and descendants whose domains are subsets of \(D_N\); it must not be transferred to a node with domain not contained in \(D_N\) unless validity is separately established there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local user cut is valid within the current node domain and compatible descendants, but cannot automatically be used elsewhere in the tree.
assumptions_latex: \(D_N\) contains all local restrictions active at node \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local validity means \(F\cap D_N\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^\top x\le b\}\).

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: User-Cut Scope Declaration
children.top_down_role: Interface metadata communicating the intended validity region of a submitted user cut.

knowledge_statements.title: User-Cut Scope Declaration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity obligation attached to a global or local cut-scope flag.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cut \(a^\top x\le b\) submitted at node \(N\), a scope declaration \(\sigma\in\{\mathrm{global},\mathrm{local}\}\) is correct only if its associated validity obligation holds. If \(\sigma=\mathrm{global}\), validity is required for every \(x\in F\), the original feasible set. If \(\sigma=\mathrm{local}\), validity is required for every \(x\in F\cap D_N\), where \(D_N\) is the current local domain, and propagation is restricted to nodes whose domains lie within \(D_N\). The declaration records a validity claim; it does not cause an otherwise invalid inequality to become valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scope flag must match the cut's proven validity domain: all original feasible points for global cuts, or the current node domain for local cuts.
assumptions_latex: The callback can identify the current node domain \(D_N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A declared scope is admissible only when its corresponding set-containment validity condition holds.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Forced User Cuts
children.top_down_role: Submission modes requesting unconditional solver admission.

knowledge_statements.title: Forced User Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admission mode requiring insertion without ordinary cut-quality filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A forced user-cut submission consists of a valid inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) and an admission instruction requiring the cut manager to insert it into the active relaxation whenever the callback state permits insertion and the cut passes mandatory correctness checks. Ordinary discretionary filters—such as efficacy, parallelism, redundancy, or pool ranking—must not be the sole reason for rejection. Forced admission does not waive validity, finite-coefficient, numerical-safety, scope, or callback-legality requirements, and it does not require permanent retention after the relaxation is subsequently reprocessed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forced cut bypasses discretionary quality filtering but still must satisfy validity, numerical, scope, and callback-legality checks; forced insertion need not mean permanent retention.
assumptions_latex: The submitted inequality is valid for its declared scope.
The solver distinguishes mandatory correctness checks from discretionary quality filters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If mandatory checks pass, \(a^\top x\le b\) is inserted despite failure of ordinary discretionary cut-quality tests.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the forced-admission leaf, but bypassing particular discretionary filters, retaining mandatory checks, and allowing later removal are solver-specific cut-manager semantics with no supporting citation.

children.title: Filterable User Cuts
children.top_down_role: Submission modes permitting solver-side rejection or deferral.

knowledge_statements.title: Filterable User Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admission mode permitting rejection by the solver's cut-quality policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A filterable user-cut submission presents a valid inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) as a candidate for admission rather than requiring insertion. After mandatory correctness and scope checks, the cut manager may accept or reject it using declared quality criteria, which may include violation, efficacy, numerical conditioning, sparsity, parallelism to existing rows, redundancy, and resource limits. Rejection of a filterable cut means only that the cut was not admitted at that opportunity; it does not imply invalidity. Acceptance likewise establishes neither facetness nor eventual permanent retention in the relaxation or cut pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A filterable cut is a valid candidate that the solver may reject for quality or resource reasons; rejection does not imply invalidity.
assumptions_latex: The inequality is valid for its declared scope.
The cut manager has a defined discretionary admission policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admission of \(a^\top x\le b\) is conditional on both mandatory checks and the discretionary filter.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the filterable-admission leaf, but the admissible quality criteria and the meanings of rejection, acceptance, and retention depend on the cut-management API and are unsupported by a source.

children.title: Admission-Mode Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice between forced and filterable submission semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Admission-Mode Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection rule separating correctness requirements from discretionary cut-management policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid submitted cut \(c\), choose forced admission only when immediate insertion is required for the callback's intended algorithmic semantics and the submitter accepts the resulting relaxation cost. Choose filterable admission when omitting \(c\) preserves correctness and the solver may trade its expected bound improvement against numerical and computational costs. Formally, if correctness of the implemented procedure requires \(c\) to be active at the present relaxation, select \(m(c)=\mathrm{forced}\); otherwise select \(m(c)=\mathrm{filterable}\). This choice does not alter the cut's validity domain or authorize using a user cut as a missing feasibility constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Force a cut only when current insertion is algorithmically required; otherwise allow filtering. The admission mode changes handling, not validity or model correctness.
assumptions_latex: The cut is valid for its declared scope.
The algorithm can determine whether omission preserves correctness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mode satisfies \(m(c)=\mathrm{forced}\) only when present insertion is required; otherwise \(m(c)=\mathrm{filterable}\).

notation.meaning: Admission mode selected for cut c.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind is appropriate for the selection leaf, but the asserted forced-versus-filterable decision rule depends on the exact solver admission contract. The prerequisite records are themselves unsourced, and no authoritative source supports the rule.

children.title: Lazy-Constraint Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Dynamic feasibility enforcement kept distinct from optional user-cut strengthening.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Candidate Lazy Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lazy enforcement of omitted model constraints at integer-feasible search candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an integer-feasible candidate \(\bar x\) for the currently loaded relaxation and a separation oracle for omitted constraints \(g_j(x)\le0\) required by the full model. Evaluate the oracle at \(\bar x\). If every required constraint satisfies \(g_j(\bar x)\le\varepsilon\), accept \(\bar x\) with respect to the lazy family. Otherwise submit one or more violated constraints with \(g_j(\bar x)>\varepsilon\) as lazy constraints, reject the candidate, and continue search after the solver incorporates them. Termination with a feasible incumbent is sound only if every integer candidate that could become incumbent is checked against the complete omitted family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check each integer candidate against all omitted required constraints; accept it only if they hold, otherwise add violated lazy constraints and reject the candidate.
assumptions_latex: The oracle detects every omitted constraint violated beyond \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
Each generated lazy constraint is valid for the full model.
The callback is invoked before an unchecked candidate becomes an incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any candidate accepted after the lazy check satisfies \(g_j(\bar x)\le\varepsilon\) for every omitted required constraint \(j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits integer-candidate lazy separation, and the completeness condition is mathematically plausible. However, callback timing, candidate rejection, lazy-row incorporation, and the guarantee that every incumbent-eligible candidate is checked are essential solver-interface claims requiring an authoritative source.

assumptions_latex: The intended feasible set is \(F=R\cap\bigcap_{c\in\mathcal L}\{x:c(x)\le 0\}\), where \(R\) is the explicitly loaded relaxation.
The solver interface permits lazy-constraint submission at a relaxation solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted relaxation point satisfies all lazy constraints separated at that invocation, while global correctness additionally requires enforcement at every integer candidate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface-level separation of omitted constraints at fractional or otherwise nonintegral relaxation points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a relaxation point \(\bar x\in R\), evaluate a separation oracle for \(\mathcal L\). If it returns constraints \(c_j(x)\le 0\) satisfying \(c_j(x)\le 0\) for every \(x\in F\) and \(c_j(\bar x)>0\), submit those constraints through the relaxation-point lazy interface and request reoptimization. If no violated constraint is found, return “no lazy constraint found” for this invocation. Because the oracle may be incomplete at fractional points, the same omitted model-defining family must still be checked at every integer candidate before acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relaxation solution, add violated omitted constraints when the interface permits it, but still check every integer candidate before declaring feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Point Lazy Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the separation leaf, and the statement is internally coherent. However, relaxation-point lazy submission, reoptimization, and integer-candidate enforcement guarantees are solver-dependent, and no inspectable citation is supplied.

assumptions_latex: The intended model has feasible set \(F=R\cap L\), but only the explicit region \(R\) is supplied initially.
A callback oracle can recognize violations of the omitted requirement set \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The static solver model represents only \(R\); correctness for \(F\) depends on complete callback enforcement of \(L\) at all acceptance points.

notation.meaning: Feasible region represented by the static model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness contract for models whose defining constraints are generated only during optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incomplete static-model interface loads constraints defining \(R\) while delegating enforcement of \(L\) to a callback, so the intended feasible set is \(F=R\cap L\). The callback must reject every solver acceptance point \(\bar x\in R\setminus L\) by supplying at least one valid omitted constraint violated by \(\bar x\). If any such point can be accepted without invoking a complete check, the implemented optimization problem is the relaxation over \(R\), not necessarily the intended problem over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When defining constraints are omitted from the static model, a complete callback must reject every candidate violating them or the solver may optimize the wrong region.
knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Static-Model Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the interface-contract leaf. The claim that callback enforcement at every acceptance point recovers the intended feasible region requires an authoritative callback-interface source; none is cited.

children.title: Lazy-Constraint Responsibilities
children.top_down_role: Model-completeness and candidate-feasibility responsibilities assigned to lazy-constraint interfaces.

assumptions_latex: The intended feasible set is \(F=R\cap\bigcap_{c\in\mathcal L}\{x:c(x)\le 0\}\).
Members of \(\mathcal L\) are necessary model constraints rather than optional relaxation-strengthening inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lazy-constraint callback must prevent acceptance of every integer candidate outside \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Obligations attached to constraints whose omission would enlarge the intended feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever the solver presents an integer candidate \(\bar x\in R\), the lazy-constraint routine must determine whether \(c(\bar x)\le 0\) for every \(c\in\mathcal L\). If some member is violated, the routine must return one or more globally valid members of \(\mathcal L\) that exclude \(\bar x\); otherwise it may certify the candidate with respect to this family. Completeness is required at candidate acceptance: failure to find an existing violated defining constraint may admit a point outside \(F\) and invalidate feasibility or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy-constraint code must completely check integer candidates and exclude every candidate violating an omitted model-defining constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Lazy-Constraint Responsibilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind matches the responsibilities leaf, and the mathematical distinction is plausible. Complete checking of every integer candidate and the precise exclusion obligation depend on the solver's lazy-constraint contract, for which no source is provided.

children.title: User-Cut Responsibilities
children.top_down_role: Relaxation-strengthening responsibilities assigned to user-cut interfaces.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation region \(R\) contains the intended feasible set \(F\).
Each generated inequality is valid for every point of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: User cuts may remove points of \(R\setminus F\) but must never remove any point of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and completeness obligations for optional relaxation-strengthening cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a relaxation point \(\bar x\in R\), a user-cut separator may return an inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) only if \(a^\top x\le b\) holds for every \(x\in F\). A returned cut should satisfy \(a^\top\bar x>b\) up to the declared numerical tolerance. The separator may be incomplete: returning no cut does not certify that \(\bar x\in F\). User cuts strengthen bounds and search performance, but candidate feasibility must be decided by the explicit model and any complete lazy-constraint or feasibility-enforcement mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: User cuts may incompletely strengthen a relaxation, but every submitted cut must be valid for all intended feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: User-Cut Responsibilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the responsibilities leaf. Global validity and optional incompleteness are standard user-cut concepts, but the claimed callback responsibilities and candidate-feasibility boundary lack an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Callback Role Classification
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for assigning a generated constraint to the appropriate callback role.

assumptions_latex: A generated inequality \(g(x)\le 0\) is considered for callback submission.
The intended feasible set is \(F\), and the loaded static region is \(R\supseteq F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The callback role is lazy exactly for necessary defining enforcement, and user-cut exactly for optional relaxation strengthening.
review_flags: exact callback permissions vary by solver
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic classification independent of solver-specific callback names.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Classify \(g(x)\le 0\) as a lazy constraint when it is valid for \(F\) and its enforcement is necessary to prevent acceptance of a point that the intended model declares infeasible. Classify it as a user cut when it is valid for \(F\), is used to remove relaxation points from \(R\setminus F\), and may be omitted without changing which integer candidates are feasible. A constraint essential to the definition of \(F\) does not become a user cut merely because it also strengthens the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify an inequality by responsibility: model-defining enforcement is lazy, while optional valid relaxation strengthening is a user cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Callback Role Classification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind appropriately expresses a classification boundary. The proposed lazy-versus-user-cut classification is plausible but relies on solver-specific meanings and permissions, and no source establishes the stated exact criterion.

children.title: Boundary Misclassification Consequences
children.top_down_role: Correctness or performance consequences of using the wrong callback role.

assumptions_latex: The static region is \(R\), the intended feasible set is \(F\subseteq R\), and callback constraints are globally valid for \(F\).
The solver applies distinct correctness contracts to lazy constraints and user cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Misclassification can invalidate correctness or degrade performance, depending on the direction of the error.
review_flags: consequences depend partly on solver callback guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure modes at the semantic boundary between defining constraints and strengthening cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a model-defining constraint is submitted only as an optional user cut, an integer point \(\bar x\in R\setminus F\) may escape separation and be accepted, making the reported solution infeasible for the intended model. If a merely strengthening inequality is submitted through a lazy interface, global validity still preserves the feasible set, but delayed enforcement or restricted callback timing may weaken bounds and increase search. In either direction, submitting an inequality not valid for all \(x\in F\) may exclude a feasible or optimal solution and destroy correctness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating defining constraints as optional cuts can admit infeasible solutions; treating strengthening cuts as lazy can impair performance, while invalid inequalities can destroy correctness.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Misclassification Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind exactly fits the terminal container. The correctness and performance consequences depend on the solver's guarantees for lazy constraints and user cuts, and no inspectable source supports the directional claims.

children.title: Constraint-Handler Separation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces in which separation is coordinated with feasibility checking, propagation, and enforcement.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Constraint handler separation and enforcement callbacks

assumptions_latex: A constraint family defines a feasible set \(C\subseteq X\).
The callback receives a solver point \(\bar x\in X\) and may add globally valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The callback either certifies that no violation was found or returns valid inequalities separating \(\bar x\) from \(C\).

notation.meaning: Set defined by the handled constraint family

review_flags: callback result codes and guarantees are implementation-specific
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract contract for separation invoked through a constraint-handler interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \(\bar x\in X\), test the handled constraint family for a violated member or derive inequalities \(a_j^\top x\le b_j\) such that \(a_j^\top x\le b_j\) for every \(x\in C\) and \(a_j^\top\bar x>b_j\) for each returned separator, within the stated tolerance. Add the separators to the permitted local or global cut store and report separation. If no separator is produced, report only the interface-prescribed “no cut found” status; this is a feasibility certificate only when the separation routine is complete for \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint separation callback examines the current point, adds valid violated inequalities, and certifies feasibility only when its separation procedure is complete.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Separation Callbacks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the callback leaf. Cut-store scope, result statuses, and when absence of a separator certifies feasibility are framework-dependent and require a constraint-handler API or manual citation.

children.title: Feasibility-Checking Responsibilities
children.top_down_role: Constraint-handler responsibilities for assessing candidate feasibility.

assumptions_latex: A handled constraint family defines \(C\subseteq X\).
The feasibility routine is invoked on a candidate \(\bar x\in X\) under a declared tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routine reports feasible exactly when every handled constraint passes its tolerance-aware predicate.

notation.meaning: Set defined by the handled constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate classification responsibility, separated from generation of enforcing constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints represented by residuals \(g_i(x)\le 0\), feasibility checking must evaluate every relevant \(g_i(\bar x)\) and report feasible precisely when \(g_i(\bar x)\le\varepsilon\) for all handled indices \(i\). If some residual exceeds \(\varepsilon\), it must report infeasibility and identify sufficient violation information for the framework's enforcement stage. The checker need not itself add a cut, branch, or modify bounds unless the interface explicitly combines checking with enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility checking classifies a candidate against every handled constraint and reports violations, without necessarily performing the action that excludes them.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Checking Responsibilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits candidate classification responsibilities. The universal residual test and required handoff of violation information assume a particular constraint-handler contract, but no authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Constraint Enforcement Responsibilities
children.top_down_role: Constraint-handler responsibilities for restoring or imposing compliance.

assumptions_latex: The feasibility checker has found a candidate \(\bar x\notin C\).
The handler can generate a valid cut, a sound domain reduction, a branching disjunction, or an infeasibility declaration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enforcement must ensure that the violating candidate cannot be accepted unchanged as feasible.

notation.meaning: Set defined by the handled constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrective responsibility after a handled constraint declares a candidate infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After detecting \(\bar x\notin C\), the enforcement routine must return a sound action that prevents acceptance of the unchanged candidate: a valid inequality violated by \(\bar x\), a valid bound tightening, a branching disjunction whose union contains \(C\), or a correct declaration that the current node contains no point of \(C\). Every action must preserve all feasible points relevant to its declared local or global scope. Returning successful enforcement without such an action violates the handler contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once a candidate violates a handled constraint, enforcement must take a sound action that prevents the unchanged candidate from being accepted.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Enforcement Responsibilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits enforcement responsibilities. The allowed actions, their local or global validity requirements, and the meaning of successful enforcement are framework-specific and unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Responsibility Transfer Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interface boundary between detecting infeasibility and initiating enforcement.

assumptions_latex: A feasibility checker classifies a candidate \(\bar x\) for a handled set \(C\).
An enforcement routine is registered to act on candidates classified as infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Responsibility transfers only after an unambiguous infeasibility result accompanied by the information required for sound enforcement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface boundary between detecting a violation and taking a solver-state-changing response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Control transfers from feasibility checking to enforcement when the checker reports \(\bar x\notin C\) under the active tolerance and supplies the violation data required by the enforcement interface. Before that transfer, the checker owns correct classification; after it, enforcement owns production of a sound excluding action or a valid declaration that no permitted action was found. A feasible or unknown checking result must not be interpreted as an enforcement request, and an infeasible result must not be treated as resolved until enforcement reports an effective action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classification responsibility ends only when a definite violation and its data are handed to enforcement; the violation remains unresolved until a sound action succeeds.
knowledge_statements.title: Responsibility Transfer Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind matches the responsibility-transfer boundary. The exact transfer trigger, ownership semantics, unknown status, and effective-action requirement require documentation for a particular constraint-handler framework.

children.title: Propagation Responsibilities
children.top_down_role: Constraint-handler responsibilities for domain inference and bound tightening.

assumptions_latex: The current node domain is a box \(D=[\ell,u]\).
Each inference is logically implied by the handled constraints together with \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Propagation may shrink \(D\) or prove it infeasible, but every inference must be locally valid for all feasible points remaining at the node.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain inference responsibility within a constraint-handler callback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(D=[\ell,u]\), derive implied bounds \(x_k\ge\ell'_k\) or \(x_k\le u'_k\) from the handled constraints and the current node assumptions. Apply only tightenings satisfying \(\ell'_k\ge\ell_k\) or \(u'_k\le u_k\) that preserve every feasible point in \(D\). Repeat until the prescribed propagation limit or a fixed point is reached. If some variable obtains \(\ell'_k>u'_k\), report node infeasibility with an explanation sufficient for the framework's inference mechanism; otherwise return the tightened domain and propagation status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation derives sound local bound tightenings, repeats to its stopping rule, and reports infeasibility when the resulting bounds conflict.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Responsibilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits propagation responsibilities. Sound bound tightening is standard, but the stopping rule, infeasibility report, and explanation requirement are framework-dependent and have no cited support.

children.title: Separation Responsibilities
children.top_down_role: Constraint-handler responsibilities for generating relaxation cuts.

assumptions_latex: A handled constraint family defines \(C\), and the current relaxation point is \(\bar x\).
Every generated inequality is valid for \(C\) in its declared local or global scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separation strengthens the relaxation by valid inequalities violated by \(\bar x\), without directly claiming domain inference.

notation.meaning: Set defined by the handled constraint family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-generation responsibility distinguished from variable-domain propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\bar x\), search for inequalities \(a_j^\top x\le b_j\) that hold for every \(x\in C\) in their declared scope and satisfy \(a_j^\top\bar x>b_j+\varepsilon\). Submit selected inequalities subject to the interface's efficacy and cut-management rules, then report whether the relaxation was modified. If no inequality is returned, report “no cut found”; unless the separator is complete, this status neither proves \(\bar x\in C\) nor authorizes acceptance of an integer candidate that still requires feasibility enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation adds valid inequalities violated by the current relaxation point; failure to find a cut is not generally a feasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation Responsibilities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits separation responsibilities. Valid violated-cut generation is coherent, but efficacy rules, modification status, and the boundary with candidate acceptance require an authoritative constraint-handler source.

children.title: Inference-to-Cut Transition
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which propagation outcomes motivate separation.

assumptions_latex: The current node relaxation is \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and its propagation domain is \(D\subseteq R\).
A propagation inference establishes \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inferred inequality may be submitted as a globally valid cut only if it holds on the global mixed-integer feasible set; otherwise its validity scope must retain the node conditions defining \(D\).

notation.meaning: Domain on which propagation proved the inference.

review_flags: Interface semantics and validity-scope rules are solver-specific; an authoritative callback-interface source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity requirement for promoting a propagation inference to a relaxation cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the global mixed-integer feasible set, let \(R\) be the current node relaxation, and let \(D\subseteq R\) encode the node bounds and propagation premises. If propagation proves \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) for all \(x\in D\), then the inequality is admissible as a cut with validity region \(V\) only when \(D\subseteq V\) and \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) holds for every feasible point in \(V\). In particular, global submission requires validity for every \(x\in F\); an inference depending on local bounds must instead be marked local and remain attached to those bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inferred inequality becomes a cut only with an explicit validity scope; globally submitted cuts must hold for every globally feasible mixed-integer point.
knowledge_statements.title: Inference-to-Cut Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the inference-to-cut leaf and its global-versus-local validity distinction is plausible, but no inspectable citation supports the solver-interface semantics, locality attachment, or admissibility rule. An authoritative constraint-handler or callback-interface source with a specific section is required.

children.title: Cut-to-Inference Transition
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which separation outcomes create propagation opportunities.

assumptions_latex: The active relaxation contains the valid row \(a^\top x\leq\beta\).
Current bounds satisfy \(\ell_i\leq x_i\leq u_i\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite residual activity yields a sound bound inference for any variable whose coefficient has the appropriate nonzero sign.

notation.meaning: Current lower and upper variable bounds.
Minimum contribution of all variables except variable j.

review_flags: The mathematical activity rule is standard, but callback ownership and propagation-registration semantics require a direct source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-activity conversion of an active cut into a bound-propagation inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a row \(a^\top x\leq\beta\), define \(m_{-j}=\sum_{i\ne j}\min\{a_i\ell_i,a_i u_i\}\). If \(a_j>0\) and \(m_{-j}>-\infty\), infer \(x_j\leq(\beta-m_{-j})/a_j\); if \(a_j<0\) and \(m_{-j}>-\infty\), infer \(x_j\geq(\beta-m_{-j})/a_j\). Intersect the inferred bound with \([\ell_j,u_j]\). Report infeasibility if the resulting interval is empty; otherwise output only a strict tightening. The inference inherits every locality condition under which the row is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute residual row activity from current bounds, derive a variable bound from a nonzero coefficient, and preserve the cut's locality conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-to-Inference Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the transition leaf, and the residual-activity formulas are mathematically standard for a valid less-than-or-equal row. However, the record also asserts callback registration, infeasibility reporting, strict-tightening, and locality-inheritance behavior without an inspectable source.

children.title: Original-Model Callback Objects
children.top_down_role: Callback-visible variables, constraints, and identifiers from the original model.

assumptions_latex: The original model is formulated in variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) before presolve transformations.
A callback API exposes stable original-model identifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An original-model callback object denotes model semantics in the \(x\)-space and must be mapped before use in a presolved relaxation.
review_flags: The precise lifetime, mutability, and admissible operations of original-model callback objects depend on the solver API.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic definition of callback objects expressed in the unpresolved model space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An original-model callback object is a callback-visible handle whose denotation is fixed in the unpresolved formulation: an original variable denotes a coordinate of \(x\), an original constraint denotes its relation in \(F_o\), and an original row denotes an inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta\). Its identity is independent of variable elimination, aggregation, bound substitution, and row deletion performed by presolve. Numerical values, activities, or cuts requested from a presolved solve are defined only after applying the interface's declared original-to-presolved mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original-model callback object refers to variables, constraints, or rows before presolve and requires an explicit mapping to interact with the active relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Model Callback Objects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the object leaf, but stable original-object identity, permitted operations, and the requirement to map before interaction with a presolved relaxation are API-specific claims. No source with a concrete locator is supplied.

children.title: Presolved-Model Callback Objects
children.top_down_role: Callback-visible variables, constraints, and identifiers from the transformed model.

assumptions_latex: Presolve produces an active formulation in variables \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
The callback is invoked in a regime exposing the active presolved relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A presolved-model callback object is interpreted directly in the active \(y\)-space and may cease to exist after a model transformation or restart.
review_flags: Object lifetime and admissible callback operations are implementation-specific and need solver-interface documentation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic definition of callback objects in the active presolved model space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A presolved-model callback object is a callback-visible handle whose denotation belongs to the active transformed formulation: a variable denotes a coordinate of \(y\), a row denotes an inequality \(c^\top y\leq\delta\), and an incumbent or relaxation solution is indexed by those transformed coordinates. Such an object is valid only for the transformation epoch and callback context in which it is exposed. It must not be identified with an original-model object unless the interface supplies a correspondence preserving the object's stated semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A presolved-model callback object belongs to the active transformed formulation and is valid only within its documented transformation epoch and callback context.
knowledge_statements.title: Presolved-Model Callback Objects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the presolved-object leaf. The asserted transformation-epoch lifetime, context validity, and treatment of transformed solution coordinates depend on a particular solver interface and cannot be validated without authoritative documentation.

children.title: Forward Model Mapping
children.top_down_role: Translation of original-model objects into presolved-model counterparts.

assumptions_latex: Presolve supplies an affine reconstruction relation \(x=Ty+t\).
The original-space expression is \(a^\top x\leq\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its forward image is \((T^\top a)^\top y\leq\beta-a^\top t\), provided the presolve correspondence is exact on the relevant feasible set.

notation.meaning: Affine reconstruction map from presolved to original variables.

review_flags: General solver presolve may require substitutions, eliminated-row certificates, or partial mappings beyond the affine case; a source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine original-to-presolved mapping for values and linear callback expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let presolve provide \(x=Ty+t\) for all presolved points under consideration. The forward value map sends \(y\) to \(x=Ty+t\). The forward expression map sends the original affine function \(a^\top x-\beta\) to \((T^\top a)^\top y+a^\top t-\beta\). Consequently, the original inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) is represented in presolved coordinates by \((T^\top a)^\top y\leq\beta-a^\top t\). Submission is permitted only if the mapping is defined for every referenced original coordinate and preserves the required global or local validity scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substitute the affine reconstruction of original variables into an original row to obtain its equivalent presolved-space row, while preserving validity scope.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward Model Mapping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the mapping leaf, and substitution through the assumed affine reconstruction gives the displayed row correctly. Source support is still required because general presolve mappings may be partial, epoch-dependent, or richer than a single affine reconstruction, and the submission rule is interface-specific.

children.title: Reverse Model Mapping
children.top_down_role: Translation of presolved callback state back to original-model objects.

assumptions_latex: Presolve uses \(x=Ty+t\) on the relevant feasible set.
A presolved-space callback row is \(c^\top y\leq\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An original-space reverse image exists only if \(T^\top a=c\) is solvable; then \(a^\top x\leq\delta+a^\top t\) agrees with the presolved row on mapped points.
review_flags: Reverse mappings can be nonunique or unavailable after aggregation; solver-specific lifting rules and certificates need a direct source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence condition for lifting a presolved linear row to original coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x=Ty+t\) and a presolved row \(c^\top y\leq\delta\), an affine original-space representative exists precisely when there is \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(T^\top a=c\). For any such \(a\), the row \(a^\top x\leq\delta+a^\top t\) restricts to \(c^\top y\leq\delta\) on mapped points. If the linear system is inconsistent, no row involving only the reconstructed original coordinates represents the presolved row exactly. If solutions are nonunique, the interface must specify a selection or equivalence convention before returning an original-model object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A presolved row can be lifted exactly only when its coefficient vector lies in the range of the transpose reconstruction map.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Model Mapping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate, but the claimed necessity of solving T^T a=c requires equality as affine functions on the full presolved coordinate space. If the relevant mapped set is lower-dimensional, exact agreement on that set may exist without coefficient equality. A source and strengthened domain hypothesis are needed before fixing the mathematical version.

children.title: Callback Threading Regimes
children.top_down_role: Single-threaded and concurrent callback execution contexts.

assumptions_latex: Each callback invocation has a context identifier \(k\) and execution interval \(I_k\).
The solver declares which invocation intervals may overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The threading regime is serial when the intervals are disjoint and concurrent when some admissible pair overlaps; concurrent regimes require per-invocation or synchronized mutable state.

notation.meaning: Execution interval of callback invocation k.

review_flags: Thread-count guarantees, callback serialization, and permitted synchronization are solver-API properties requiring authoritative documentation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of callback execution by possible temporal overlap of invocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For invocation set \(K\), let \(I_k\) be the execution interval of invocation \(k\). The callback threading regime is serial if \(I_k\cap I_\ell=\varnothing\) for every distinct \(k,\ell\in K\). It is concurrent if the execution contract permits \(I_k\cap I_\ell\ne\varnothing\) for some pair. A concurrent regime is thread-local when each invocation accesses a disjoint mutable state component \(S_k\); it is shared-state when distinct invocations may access the same mutable component of \(S\). Correctness in the shared-state regime requires synchronization or an operation whose result is invariant under every permitted interleaving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Callback threading is serial when invocations cannot overlap and concurrent when they may; shared mutable state then needs synchronization or interleaving-invariant operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Callback Threading Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the threading-regimes leaf, and the interval classification is internally coherent. Whether invocations may overlap, what state is shared, and which synchronization mechanisms are permitted are solver and runtime contract claims with no cited source.

children.title: Deterministic Callback Execution
children.top_down_role: Execution constraints supporting reproducible callback outcomes.

assumptions_latex: The initial model, parameters, random seeds, and callback inputs are fixed.
The callback and solver use deterministic arithmetic and deterministic tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Callback execution is deterministic when every admissible schedule yields the same ordered callback effects and the same solver-visible outputs.

notation.meaning: Set of schedules admitted by the execution regime.
Observable callback-and-solver trace under schedule sigma.

review_flags: Actual reproducibility guarantees and the set of observable effects vary by solver and require an authoritative interface source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedule-invariance criterion for deterministic callback execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix initial data \(d\), including the model, parameters, callback code, seeds, and external inputs. Let \(\Sigma(d)\) be the schedules allowed by the callback execution contract, and let \(\mathcal{T}(\sigma)\) record solver-visible callback events, submitted rows, bound changes, abort decisions, and returned values. Execution is deterministic if \(\mathcal{T}(\sigma_1)=\mathcal{T}(\sigma_2)\) for all \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\Sigma(d)\). Serial invocation alone is insufficient unless event ordering, numerical reductions, tie-breaking, and every callback dependency on mutable or external state are also deterministic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With all inputs fixed, callback execution is deterministic exactly when every permitted schedule produces the same observable callback effects and solver outputs.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Callback Execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the deterministic-execution leaf, and schedule-invariance is a coherent criterion. The observable trace, admissible schedules, arithmetic behavior, and reproducibility guarantees are interface-specific and lack an authoritative citation with a precise locator.

children.title: Concurrency-Induced Nondeterminism
children.top_down_role: Reproducibility risks arising from callback scheduling and shared state.

assumptions_latex: Two concurrent invocations produce distinct valid cuts \(r_1\) and \(r_2\).
A shared cut budget accepts only the first submitted cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Different legal schedules can accept different cuts, so the callback trace and subsequent search need not be deterministic.

notation.meaning: Distinct cuts produced by concurrent invocations.
Schedule in which invocation i submits first.
Set of accepted cuts under a schedule.

review_flags: The example is mathematically concrete, but whether a solver exposes this race depends on its callback serialization and cut-queue policy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal race showing schedule-dependent cut acceptance under concurrent callbacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose concurrent invocations compute distinct valid cuts \(r_1\) and \(r_2\), and a shared budget admits exactly one cut by first-arrival order. Under schedule \(\sigma_1\), the first invocation submits before the second, giving \(A(\sigma_1)=\{r_1\}\). Under schedule \(\sigma_2\), the order is reversed, giving \(A(\sigma_2)=\{r_2\}\). Hence \(A(\sigma_1)\ne A(\sigma_2)\) despite identical model data and individually deterministic callback computations. Because the accepted relaxation differs, node bounds, branching choices, and later callback inputs may also differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a first-arrival cut budget, reversing two concurrent submissions changes the accepted cut and can alter the subsequent branch-and-cut search.
knowledge_statements.title: Concurrency-Induced Nondeterminism

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind correctly matches a nondeterminism leaf, and the first-arrival example is logically valid under its assumptions. No source establishes that the relevant callback regime can concurrently submit into such a first-arrival budget, so its applicability to the stated interface remains unsupported.

children.title: Callback Reentrancy
children.top_down_role: Execution contexts where callback code may be entered again before prior work is complete.

assumptions_latex: Callback invocations may overlap or nest on one callback object.
Each invocation receives a distinct context \(c_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The callback is reentrant when overlapping invocations cannot corrupt one another's state or make an invocation depend on another's partial execution.

notation.meaning: Output of the callback for a context.
Private state owned by invocation k.

review_flags: The solver's definition of reentrancy, nesting possibilities, and callback-safe operations requires interface documentation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavioral reentrancy criterion for overlapping or nested callback invocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A callback implementation \(f\) is reentrant on admissible contexts if, whenever invocations with contexts \(c_k\) overlap or nest, each invocation uses private state \(S_k\) or synchronized shared state and returns the same solver-visible result it would return under an isolated execution with \(c_k\). No invocation may retain an unsafely shared temporary, overwrite another invocation's context, or call an operation forbidden during callback execution. Reentrancy concerns safe overlap of active invocations; it does not by itself imply that the resulting multi-invocation trace is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A callback is reentrant when overlapping or nested calls preserve each call's isolated behavior through private or correctly synchronized state.
knowledge_statements.title: Callback Reentrancy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is suitable for this leaf, but the statement combines a general isolated-execution criterion with solver-specific restrictions on nesting and callback-safe operations. An authoritative interface source is needed to determine the exact admissible contexts and operations.

children.title: Callback State Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership and lifetime boundaries for callback-maintained state.

assumptions_latex: The mutable callback state decomposes as \(S=S_0\times\prod_{k\in K}S_k\).
Invocation \(k\) is assigned exclusive ownership of \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each invocation may mutate only its owned component; mutations of shared component \(S_0\) require a declared atomic or synchronized protocol.

notation.meaning: State component exclusively owned by invocation k.

review_flags: Ownership transfer, object lifetime, and permitted mutations are implementation-specific and need an authoritative source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ownership discipline for mutable state used by callback invocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the mutable state be \(S=S_0\times\prod_{k\in K}S_k\), where \(S_0\) is shared and \(S_k\) is owned by invocation \(k\). During its lifetime, invocation \(k\) may read and write \(S_k\), may not access \(S_\ell\) for \(\ell\ne k\), and may modify \(S_0\) only through an operation declared atomic or protected by a synchronization protocol. Ownership transfer is valid only at a synchronization point after the former owner has ceased access. Callback-context handles owned by the solver must not be retained beyond their declared lifetime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Give each invocation exclusive mutable state, synchronize every shared mutation, and transfer ownership only after the previous owner has stopped accessing the object.
knowledge_statements.title: Callback State Ownership

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the state-ownership leaf. The ownership discipline is plausible, but handle lifetime, transfer points, atomic operations, and permitted mutation are implementation and language-runtime properties that have no cited support.

children.title: Shared-State Isolation
children.top_down_role: Isolation of mutable state across callback invocations or worker contexts.

assumptions_latex: Concurrent invocations have private states \(S_k\) and access shared state \(S_0\) through operations \(g\).
The required callback result is specified independently for each invocation context.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shared state is isolated when private writes are disjoint and shared operations are linearizable or commute for every permitted interleaving.
review_flags: The isolation mechanisms and memory-consistency guarantees available inside callbacks require solver and language-runtime sources.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolation predicate preventing callback interleavings from exposing partial or conflicting state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Shared-state isolation holds if each invocation \(k\) writes only its private component \(S_k\), and every operation on \(S_0\) is either read-only over an immutable snapshot or linearizable with respect to a specified sequential operation. Alternatively, unsynchronized shared updates are admissible only when their operations commute and associate on all reachable states, so every permitted interleaving has the same specified effect. An invocation must not observe another invocation's partial update. Objects published from \(S_k\) to \(S_0\) must be fully initialized before publication and immutable thereafter unless subsequent mutation is synchronized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isolation requires disjoint private writes and shared operations that are snapshot-based, linearizable, or order-independent, with no exposure of partial updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-State Isolation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the isolation leaf. Linearizability is a sound isolation mechanism, but commutativity and associativity alone do not generally establish the claimed result when operations return values or have other observable effects. Solver and memory-model sources are required to specify the observations and sufficient synchronization conditions.

children.title: Nested-Invocation Hazards
children.top_down_role: Correctness risks caused by nested or overlapping callback execution.

assumptions_latex: A solver may invoke a separation callback recursively or concurrently before an earlier invocation has returned.
The callback reads or mutates invocation-dependent state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correctness requires invocation-local state or synchronization that makes each state transition serializable; otherwise callback behavior is not defined by the current relaxation point alone.

notation.meaning: relaxation point supplied to invocation k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addresses semantic failure caused by nested callback execution, independently of any particular solver API.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let invocation \(k\) receive point \(x^{(k)}\) and access mutable state \(s_k\). A nested invocation \(\ell\) is hazardous when it occurs before \(k\) returns and both invocations access a shared object \(s\), with at least one write, without a synchronization order. If the cut returned by \(k\) can then depend on whether \(\ell\) occurred, the callback is not a function of \(x^{(k)}\) and its declared inputs. Correct execution therefore requires disjoint invocation-local states, immutable shared state, or synchronization yielding a serializable order of state transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested callbacks are hazardous when overlapping invocations mutate shared state and thereby make a returned cut depend on execution order rather than declared inputs.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Invocation Hazards

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary and content kind fit the leaf, but solver-independent claims about nested callback execution and required synchronization need an authoritative callback or concurrency source.

assumptions_latex: The candidate inequality is \(a^T x\le b\), with \(a\in\mathbb R^n\).
All quantities are evaluated in the callback's declared model coordinate system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The callback reports violation only when \(v(x)>\tau_{\mathrm{sep}}(a,b)\), and accepts feasibility only when \(v(x)\le\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}(a,b)\), with an explicit policy for the undecided band.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scale-aware acceptance and rejection predicates for callback-generated linear cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate cut \(a^T x\le b\), define \(v(x)=a^T x-b\) and nonnegative, scale-aware thresholds \(\tau_{\mathrm{sep}}(a,b)\ge\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}(a,b)\). The callback may declare the cut violated only if \(v(x)>\tau_{\mathrm{sep}}(a,b)\), and may declare it satisfied only if \(v(x)\le\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}(a,b)\). Values satisfying \(\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}(a,b)<v(x)\le\tau_{\mathrm{sep}}(a,b)\) form an ambiguity band and must receive an explicit policy, such as reevaluation at higher precision or no cut submission. Both thresholds must scale consistently under positive rescaling of \((a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A callback should separate only beyond a scale-aware violation threshold and explicitly handle points lying between feasibility and separation thresholds.
knowledge_statements.title: Callback Numerical Tolerances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the tolerance leaf and is internally coherent, but the two-threshold policy is implementation-sensitive and has no supporting numerical-interface source.

children.title: Separation Failure Control System
children.top_down_role: Mathematical, numerical, algorithmic, and interface boundaries at which separation or cut management becomes unreliable or counterproductive.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Cut selection, efficacy, density, separation limits, and cut-pool controls

assumptions_latex: A rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is represented by a polynomial-size encoding.
A separation oracle must either return a violated valid inequality or certify membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If exact optimization over \(P\) is NP-hard, polynomial-time exact separation over \(P\) would imply polynomial-time optimization; hence exact separation is intractable unless the corresponding complexity classes collapse.

notation.meaning: encoded rational polyhedron or integer hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the rational-polyhedral, polynomial-encoding form of optimization-separation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact separation algorithm for \(P\) receives a rational point \(\bar x\) and either certifies \(\bar x\in P\) or returns rational \((a,b)\) such that \(a^T x\le b\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(a^T\bar x>b\). Under the standard rational encoding and polynomial bit-complexity model, polynomial-time exact separation and polynomial-time linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomially interreducible. Consequently, for any family whose exact linear optimization problem is NP-hard, a polynomial-time exact separator would yield a polynomial-time algorithm for that optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For rational polyhedra, exact separation is polynomially equivalent to linear optimization, so NP-hard optimization families generally have intractable exact separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Intractable Exact Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity role fits, but optimization–separation equivalence requires precise oracle, encoding, rationality, and bit-complexity hypotheses. No source is supplied to verify that the stated formulation has sufficient hypotheses.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the target feasible region.
\(\mathcal F\) is a prescribed family of inequalities valid for \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is weak on \(Q\) when some exterior point in \(Q\setminus P\) satisfies every inequality in \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weakness relative to a relaxation, not merely poor empirical performance.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a family of inequalities \(a^T x\le b\) valid for \(P\). Its induced closure on \(Q\) is \(Q_{\mathcal F}=Q\cap\bigcap_{(a,b)\in\mathcal F}\{x:a^T x\le b\}\). The separator family is weak on \(Q\) if \(Q_{\mathcal F}\supsetneq P\); equivalently, there exists \(\bar x\in Q\setminus P\) that violates no inequality in \(\mathcal F\). Weakness is relative to both \(P\) and \(Q\), and does not imply that individual inequalities in \(\mathcal F\) are invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separator family is weak when its entire closure still contains an infeasible point of the current relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Separator Families

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

assumptions_latex: Every inequality returned by the heuristic is valid for \(P\).
The heuristic searches only a subset of the available valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A null heuristic response does not certify membership in \(P\) unless the procedure is complete for the declared inequality class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes sound cut generation from completeness of the separation search.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a sound heuristic separator: whenever \(H(\bar x)=(a,b)\), the inequality \(a^T x\le b\) is valid for every \(x\in P\) and satisfies \(a^T\bar x>b\). If \(H\) is not complete, then \(H(\bar x)=\varnothing\) implies only that its search found no violated inequality. It does not imply \(\bar x\in P\), nor that no valid separating inequality exists. Membership certification from a null response is justified only when completeness has been established for the claimed region or inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of a heuristic to find a cut is not evidence that the query point is feasible or unseparable.
knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic Nonseparation Without Certification

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

assumptions_latex: The computed violation \(\widehat v\) approximates the exact value \(v=a^T\bar x-b\).
A certified error bound \(\eta\ge0\) satisfies \(|\widehat v-v|\le\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separation is certified only if \(\widehat v-\eta>0\), satisfaction only if \(\widehat v+\eta\le0\), and otherwise the sign is ambiguous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes ambiguity through a certified forward-error interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the cut \(a^T x\le b\) at \(\bar x\), suppose the computed residual \(\widehat v\) satisfies \(|\widehat v-(a^T\bar x-b)|\le\eta\). Then the exact residual lies in \([\widehat v-\eta,\widehat v+\eta]\). A violation is certified only when \(\widehat v-\eta>0\), while satisfaction is certified only when \(\widehat v+\eta\le0\). If \(\widehat v-\eta\le0<\widehat v+\eta\), both signs are consistent with the numerical information, so accepting or rejecting the cut solely from \(\widehat v\) is unjustified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near violation is ambiguous when the error interval around the computed residual contains zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Violation Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-sign condition is mathematically precise and fits the leaf, but no inspectable numerical-analysis source supports the certified-error interpretation.

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts associated with unstable or poorly conditioned relaxation behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses local sign sensitivity of a linear-inequality residual as the conditioning criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on coefficient vectors and \(\|\cdot\|_*\) its dual norm. For cut data \((a,b)\neq(0,0)\), define \(r(x)=a^T x-b\), \(D(x)=\|a\|\,\|x\|_*+|b|\), and \(\rho(x)=|r(x)|/D(x)\) whenever \(D(x)>0\). Under perturbations satisfying \(\|\Delta a\|\le\varepsilon\|a\|\) and \(|\Delta b|\le\varepsilon|b|\), the residual sign is guaranteed to remain unchanged when \(\rho(x)>\varepsilon\). Classification is nonrobust when \(\rho(x)\le\varepsilon\): an admissible perturbation can reach the zero boundary, and when \(\rho(x)<\varepsilon\), an admissible perturbation can reverse the sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut is locally ill-conditioned when admissible small relative data perturbations can bring its residual to zero or reverse its sign.
assumptions_latex: The cut is represented as \(a^T x\le b\), with \((a,b)\neq(0,0)\).
Coefficient perturbations are measured in a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and points use its dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\).
The scale denominator \(\|a\|\,\|x\|_*+|b|\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\rho(x)>\varepsilon\), every admissible perturbation preserves the residual sign; if \(\rho(x)\le\varepsilon\), classification can reach the decision boundary, with strict sign reversal possible when \(\rho(x)<\varepsilon\).

children.title: Large-Coefficient Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts whose coefficient scale creates numerical reliability concerns.

assumptions_latex: The cut \(a^T x\le b\) is stored in finite precision.
A positive normalization convention is fixed before coefficients are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large-coefficient status must be defined after normalization and indicates risk of overflow, rounding amplification, or loss of small coefficients, not invalidity of the exact inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coefficient largeness relative to a normalization and implementation threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a normalization \((\tilde a,\tilde b)=\lambda(a,b)\) with \(\lambda>0\), and let \(M>0\) be the implementation's reliable-magnitude threshold. The cut is large-coefficient under this convention when \(L=\max\{\|\tilde a\|_\infty,|\tilde b|\}>M\). Because positive scaling preserves the exact halfspace, largeness is not intrinsic without normalization. It is a numerical warning: finite-precision storage or evaluation may overflow, amplify absolute rounding error, or eliminate materially smaller coefficients. Large-coefficient status alone does not show that the exact cut is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut has large coefficients only relative to normalization and machine limits; the warning concerns numerical representation, not exact validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Large-Coefficient Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized warning condition fits the leaf, but the claimed finite-precision consequences and reliable-magnitude threshold are implementation-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Conditioning-Scale Interaction
children.top_down_role: Numerical risk arising when poor conditioning coincides with extreme coefficient scale.

assumptions_latex: Two representations \((a,b)\) and \((\lambda a,\lambda b)\) with \(\lambda>0\) define the same exact halfspace.
Residuals and absolute tolerances are evaluated in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioning diagnostics and violation tests must be scale invariant or use a prescribed normalization; otherwise equivalent cut representations can receive different decisions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the invariance requirement linking cut scaling, conditioning, and numerical acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Positive scaling changes the residual from \(r(x)=a^T x-b\) to \(r_\lambda(x)=\lambda r(x)\) while leaving the exact halfspace unchanged. Therefore the absolute test \(r(x)>\tau\) with fixed \(\tau\) is representation dependent: an equivalent scaling may change its outcome. A coherent cut interface must normalize \((a,b)\) before testing, or use a threshold \(\tau(a,b,x)\) satisfying \(\tau(\lambda a,\lambda b,x)=\lambda\tau(a,b,x)\). Scale invariance does not remove ill-conditioning, but prevents arbitrary rescaling from changing the reported violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent positive scalings must produce the same cut decision, requiring normalization or a tolerance that scales with the coefficients.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning-Scale Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scale-invariance property is coherent and appropriately classified, but no source supports its use as an interface requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Cut Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard floating-point error model for multiplication and sequential accumulation of a dot product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cut with \(n\) nonzero coefficients, assume each multiplication and addition in sequential evaluation is rounded in floating-point arithmetic. Then \(|\operatorname{fl}(a^T x)-a^T x|\le\gamma_n|a|^T|x|\), where \(\gamma_n=nu/(1-nu)\) and \(nu<1\). Increasing density raises the worst-case accumulation factor and can increase the magnitude sum. If \(|a^T x-b|\) is no larger than a valid bound for the combined dot-product and final-subtraction errors, the violation sign is numerically unresolved. Severe cancellation can cause this even when individual coefficients are moderate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense cuts can accumulate substantial rounding error, and cancellation can make a small violation numerically unresolved.
assumptions_latex: The cut has \(n\) nonzero coefficients, and each multiplication and addition used to evaluate \(a^T x\) is rounded with unit roundoff \(u\).
No overflow or underflow occurs, and \(nu<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense-cut evaluation uncertainty can grow proportionally to \(\gamma_n|a|^T|x|\), so a residual comparable to the full evaluation-error bound has an unresolved sign.

assumptions_latex: The intended feasible set is \(P\), and the submitted inequality is \(a^T x\le b\).
The implementation relaxes or perturbs the inequality using a numerical tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity is lost whenever the effective submitted halfspace excludes some point of \(P\), even if the exclusion is smaller than the solver's feasibility tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact cut validity from a solver's tolerance-based feasibility classification.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact cut \(a^T x\le b\) is valid for \(P\) precisely when \(\sup_{x\in P}a^T x\le b\). If tolerance handling effectively submits the stronger inequality \(a^T x\le b-\delta\) with \(\delta>0\), validity is lost whenever \(b-\delta<\sup_{x\in P}a^T x\le b\). A feasibility tolerance applied later by the solver does not restore exact validity. Therefore tolerances used to detect violation must not be converted into unverified inward shifts of a valid halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Turning a detection tolerance into an inward cut shift can exclude feasible points and destroy exact validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Induced Validity Loss

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

assumptions_latex: A cutting-plane process generates relaxation bounds \(L_0,L_1,\ldots\) for a minimization problem.
The bounds are nondecreasing and bounded above by a valid upper bound \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tailing off over a window occurs when recent normalized bound gains are uniformly small while the certified optimality gap remains larger than the target tolerance.

notation.meaning: relaxation lower bound after round k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an operational, scale-normalized stagnation condition for minimization cutting-plane rounds.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a window length \(m\ge1\), gain threshold \(\varepsilon>0\), and unresolved-gap threshold \(\tau>0\). At round \(k\ge m\), tailing off is present when \(U-L_k>\tau\) and \((L_i-L_{i-1})/\max\{1,|L_{i-1}|\}\le\varepsilon\) for every \(i=k-m+1,\ldots,k\). This condition records persistent negligible relaxation improvement despite a material certified gap. It is a stagnation diagnostic, not a certificate that no stronger valid cut exists or that convergence has failed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tailing off means several consecutive cut rounds make negligible normalized bound progress while a material optimality gap remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Tailing Off

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operational condition is internally defined and fits the leaf, but the cited numerical-results section does not establish this particular windowed definition of tailing off. A source supporting the diagnostic is required.

children.title: Relaxation Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Stagnation associated with degenerate relaxation solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Degeneracy
